# A Note on AI Assistance {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-warning title="Working draft: Unverified text"}
**This text is an active, evolving work in progress.** This book will ultimately undergo the exact same rigorous, line-by-line human expert review that grounded earlier foundational texts in this curriculum, but it has not reached that stage yet. It is shared openly as an early draft to invite community critique and collective refinement.
:::

This book is released as an open-access, living textbook; it is not yet under contract with a commercial publisher. Because the systems architecture for agentic and autonomous machine learning is moving week by week, I am sharing these chapters as an open research notebook rather than holding them back for a multi-year publishing cycle.

Every textbook begins not with polished prose, but with collecting ideas, organizing scattered concepts, and structuring outlines: deciding what needs to be a chapter, what belongs in a section, what needs explaining, and crucially, what not to cover. In developing this text, I used artificial intelligence to help explore how to structure the pieces together, discover relevant literature, and organize the resulting curriculum.

Given that this book is about agentic systems, I also experimented directly with agentic workflows during the authoring process. I attempted to orchestrate multi-step agentic pipelines to assist in drafting and organizing sections of the curriculum. Those attempts failed decisively, demonstrating firsthand why unconstrained autonomous agents can not replace human synthesis. Yet that failure was profoundly instructive. Setting up guardrails, context boundaries, and alignment mechanisms to help models collaborate constructively with me provided immediate, practical insight into the exact systems challenges this book analyzes. I used this process to learn firsthand how to design, constrain, and steer agentic workflows when curating complex, unfamiliar subject matter.

A textbook is fundamentally a distillation; the primary credit belongs to the researchers whose papers made the foundational discoveries and whose work populates our bibliography. At the same time, tools do not write textbooks. Assembling those discoveries into a coherent, teachable systems narrative has required months of demanding labor, late nights, and iterative rewriting: defining the abstractions, designing the architecture of the stochastic computer, constructing executable simulation models, and refining draft material. The architectural vision, the labor, and the choices are mine.

Because foundation models generate outputs probabilistically and can produce persuasive yet subtly flawed formulations, **this unverified draft must be read with healthy skepticism**. While the embedded code cells execute and the automated test suite checks reference hygiene, the conceptual frameworks have not yet undergone the deep, one-on-one human expert validation that will precede final publication. I encourage readers, practitioners, and researchers to read critically, report flaws on GitHub, challenge our formulations, and help us shape this draft into a verified foundation for the field.

The core standard remains unchanged: **the tool can propose, but only the human engineer can ratify and take responsibility.**
